**[I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY]{.underline}**

The purpose of this memorandum is to recommend that the Board of Directors of Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. (\"Verimark\" or the \"Company\") authorize the undersigned counsel to negotiate and accept a settlement of the above-captioned litigation in the range of **\$75 million to \$95 million** in monetary consideration, together with substantial non-monetary relief, at the mediation session scheduled for March 14--15, 2024. This recommendation is based on a thorough assessment of the litigation posture, probability-weighted damages analysis, collectibility constraints, litigation-cost exposure, and the strategic value of the non-monetary components of the proposed settlement.

The litigation arises from a systematic, years-long scheme by Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC (\"Coastal Palms\") and its affiliates to underreport Gross Room Revenue (\"GRR\") across 22 franchised hotel properties operating under the Verimark Suites and Verimark Select brands. The underreporting was accomplished primarily through the use of a related entity, Suncoast Room Management Inc. (\"Suncoast\"), to collect and divert revenues from direct bookings --- including walk-in guests, corporate-direct contracts, and bookings made through the gulfcoastrooms.com website --- outside of the GRR calculation reported to Verimark. This scheme resulted in an estimated \$197.8 million in underreported GRR over the 2013--2021 period, and corresponding underpayments of royalties, marketing-fund contributions, and technology fees totaling approximately \$16.1 million in direct underpayments, with additional claims for contractual late-payment interest and liquidated damages bringing Verimark\'s total claimed damages to approximately \$150 million.

Verimark\'s litigation position was substantially strengthened by the Court\'s February 9, 2024 Order granting Verimark\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on Counts I and II. The Court found that Coastal Palms\' systematic exclusion of Suncoast-collected revenues from GRR constituted a material breach of Sections 4.1 and 4.2 of the Franchise License Agreements (\"FLAs\") as a matter of law. This ruling establishes liability on the two principal breach-of-contract counts, leaving only the damages determination for trial. The Court also denied Coastal Palms\' Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment in its entirety, including on its \$12 million counterclaim.

Mediation is scheduled for March 14--15, 2024, before the Honorable Patricia Everwood (Ret.) at Everwood Dispute Resolution PLLC in Coral Gables, Florida. The parties agreed to mediate on February 23, 2024, following the summary judgment ruling. This represents a meaningful opportunity to resolve this matter on favorable terms before incurring the substantial additional costs of a May 2024 trial.

Our recommended settlement package includes the following key components:

> • **Monetary Consideration:** \$75 million to \$95 million, with a target settlement at or near \$87.5 million (the midpoint of the authority range);
>
> • **Cash Payment at Closing:** \$25 million funded via wire transfer from an Ironclad National Bank escrow account;
>
> • **Structured Payments:** Balance of \$62.5 million (at the \$87.5 million target) paid in eight semi-annual installments of \$7.8125 million each, with 6.5% per annum simple interest on the outstanding balance;
>
> • **Franchise Surrender:** Coastal Palms to surrender franchise rights to 14 of 22 properties, with a 120-day de-identification period;
>
> • **Enhanced Audit Protocols:** Quarterly audits, real-time POS integration, and cost-shifting to Coastal Palms for a five-year period at the 8 retained properties;
>
> • **Personal Guaranties:** From Randall Brecker and Nolan Prescott for the full structured-payment amount;
>
> • **First-Priority Security Interest:** On 8 unencumbered hotel properties with an aggregate appraised value of \$71.2 million;
>
> • **Mutual Release:** Broad mutual release of all claims through the effective date, with dismissal of Coastal Palms\' counterclaim with prejudice; and
>
> • **Confidentiality and Non-Disparagement:** Subject to Verimark\'s SEC disclosure obligations.

The recommended settlement range of \$75 million to \$95 million reflects a carefully calibrated assessment that accounts for: (i) the probability-weighted damages analysis yielding a range of approximately \$70 million to \$105 million, with a midpoint of approximately \$85 million; (ii) the significant litigation risks that remain with respect to damages quantification, particularly the enforceability of the FLA\'s liquidated-damages provision under Florida\'s penalty doctrine; (iii) the projected additional litigation costs of \$1.0 million to \$2.2 million through trial, and \$500,000 to \$1.0 million for appellate proceedings; (iv) the collectibility constraints imposed by Ironclad National Bank\'s approximately \$94 million in first-lien mortgage loans on 18 of the 22 properties; (v) the risk that aggressive post-judgment enforcement could trigger a Coastal Palms bankruptcy filing, which would substantially impair Verimark\'s recovery; and (vi) the significant non-monetary value --- estimated at \$15 million to \$25 million in net present value over a 10-year horizon --- of the franchise-surrender and re-franchising opportunity.

In our judgment, a settlement within the recommended range, coupled with the non-monetary relief described herein, delivers a total value to Verimark that compares favorably to the expected value of proceeding through trial, while providing the certainty of recovery that a litigated outcome cannot guarantee. We respectfully request that the Board approve the recommended settlement authority in advance of the March 14--15 mediation, and that it authorize Priya Anand to accept any settlement within the \$75 million to \$95 million range at mediation without the need to recess for further Board approval, in order to maintain negotiating momentum and credibility with the mediator and opposing counsel.

The investigation that ultimately gave rise to this litigation was triggered by a whistleblower report submitted to Verimark\'s compliance hotline on November 8, 2021. The report was made by Janet Kerrigan, a former regional controller for Coastal Palms who had been terminated by Coastal Palms in October 2021. Ms. Kerrigan reported that Coastal Palms had been systematically diverting revenues through Suncoast Room Management Inc. and excluding those revenues from the GRR calculations reported to Verimark. Her report included specific allegations regarding the use of the gulfcoastrooms.com direct-booking website, corporate-direct contracts managed through Suncoast, and walk-in cash payments that were processed outside of the Verimark-integrated property management system.

Upon receipt of the Kerrigan report, Verimark\'s compliance team conducted an initial internal review and promptly escalated the matter to the General Counsel\'s office. On November 22, 2021, Verimark retained Thornbury & Associates CPAs LLP (\"Thornbury\"), led by audit partner Malcolm Thornbury, CPA, to conduct a comprehensive franchise-compliance audit of the top 10 Coastal Palms properties ranked by reported GRR. This engagement was structured to examine the 2019--2021 reporting period across those 10 properties and to determine whether the allegations in the Kerrigan report could be corroborated through financial records.

On January 18, 2022, Thornbury delivered its preliminary findings. The results were striking. Across the 10 audited properties, Thornbury determined that GRR had been underreported by approximately 26% for the 2019--2021 period. The principal mechanism for this underreporting was confirmed to be the Suncoast revenue-collection arrangement described in the Kerrigan report, supplemented by improper netting of online travel agency (\"OTA\") payments against GRR.

Thornbury extrapolated its findings across all 22 Coastal Palms properties and across the full contractual period from 2013 through 2021, estimating total underreported GRR of approximately \$197.8 million. While the extrapolation necessarily involved assumptions regarding properties and time periods not directly audited, the methodology was conservative and was subsequently validated by the more comprehensive forensic analysis conducted by Dr. Sharon Kettlewell of Ridgeline Forensic Advisory LLC during the litigation.

On February 4, 2022, armed with the Thornbury preliminary findings, Verimark issued a formal Notice of Material Breach to Coastal Palms pursuant to Section 14.1 of the FLAs. The Notice demanded that Coastal Palms cure the identified breaches within 30 days by, among other things, providing a full accounting of all Suncoast-collected revenues, paying all underpaid royalties and marketing-fund contributions together with accrued interest, and implementing immediate corrective measures to ensure accurate GRR reporting going forward.

On February 28, 2022, the law firm of Whitfield, Barrow & Crane LLP, acting through Nathan Whitfield III, Senior Partner, responded on behalf of Coastal Palms. The response denied any material breach, asserting that Suncoast\'s revenues were not properly included in the FLA definition of GRR and that Coastal Palms\' reporting practices were consistent with industry custom and the parties\' course of dealing over the nine-year franchise relationship. The response made no offer to cure and provided no accounting of Suncoast revenues.

The 30-day cure period expired on March 6, 2022, with no cure having been tendered by Coastal Palms.

**[B. Litigation Timeline Highlights]{.underline}**

On March 7, 2022, the day after expiration of the cure period, Verimark filed its Complaint in the Circuit Court of the 17th Judicial Circuit, Broward County, Florida. The Complaint asserted ten counts against Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC and its affiliated entities, including breach of contract (royalties), breach of contract (marketing-fund contributions), breach of contract (technology fees), fraudulent concealment, civil conspiracy, aiding and abetting breach of fiduciary duty, unjust enrichment, declaratory judgment, accounting, and tortious interference with contractual relations. Calderwood & Harkness LLP was retained as litigation counsel simultaneously with the filing.

On April 18, 2022, Coastal Palms, through Whitfield, Barrow & Crane LLP, filed its Answer and Affirmative Defenses, denying the material allegations of the Complaint and raising fifteen affirmative defenses including waiver, estoppel, laches, unclean hands, failure to mitigate, and contractual ambiguity regarding the GRR definition. Coastal Palms simultaneously filed a \$12 million Counterclaim against Verimark alleging brand-standard violations at certain Verimark Suites and Verimark Select properties, claiming that Verimark had failed to maintain brand quality and had over-billed Coastal Palms for technology-system upgrades and property-improvement plan requirements.

The Case Management Conference was held on June 14, 2022, before the Honorable Judge Calloway. The Court set an aggressive schedule for discovery and trial preparation, with trial originally set for February 2024. The Court entered a Confidentiality and Protective Order governing the production of proprietary financial information by both parties and non-party Suncoast Room Management Inc.

Discovery in this case was extensive and hard-fought. Verimark propounded comprehensive document requests targeting Coastal Palms\' financial records, Suncoast\'s banking and operational records, and communications between Coastal Palms\' principals and its property-management and accounting personnel. Coastal Palms\' initial document production of approximately 84,000 documents was served on August 22, 2022. However, that production was woefully incomplete, omitting virtually all records relating to Suncoast\'s operations and revenues.

Verimark was compelled to file a Motion to Compel on September 16, 2022, seeking production of all Suncoast financial records, including bank statements, merchant processing records, OTA settlement statements, and the gulfcoastrooms.com booking data. The Court granted the Motion to Compel on October 28, 2022, ordering production within 21 days and rejecting Coastal Palms\' arguments that Suncoast was a non-party entity outside its control. The Court specifically found that Coastal Palms exercised sufficient control over Suncoast --- whose sole officer, Randall Brecker, was also the 60% equity holder and managing member of Coastal Palms --- to warrant a finding that Suncoast\'s records were within Coastal Palms\' possession, custody, or control.

Following the Court\'s order, an additional 312,000 documents were produced, including Suncoast bank records, OTA reconciliation reports, and property-management system (\"PMS\") data. In total, Nexagen Document Solutions LLC processed approximately 2.3 million documents comprising approximately 1.1 terabytes of data, utilizing predictive coding and technology-assisted review to identify and prioritize the most relevant materials. The total document production across all parties ultimately comprised approximately 396,000 documents.

Fact depositions were conducted between January 9 and March 17, 2023. Fourteen witnesses were deposed, including Randall Brecker (two days), Nolan Prescott, Theresa Brecker, Janet Kerrigan, six property-level general managers, two Coastal Palms accounting personnel, and two Verimark franchise-operations executives. Expert depositions were taken on June 26--27, 2023, covering Dr. Sharon Kettlewell (Verimark\'s damages expert) and Professor Grant Hargrove (Coastal Palms\' damages expert).

Discovery closed on August 4, 2023, following the completion of the expert phase and resolution of several remaining discovery disputes through a telephonic conference with Judge Calloway\'s chambers.

**[C. Summary Judgment Rulings]{.underline}**

On September 29, 2023, Verimark filed its Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on Counts I and II of the Complaint --- the breach-of-contract claims relating to underpaid royalties and marketing-fund contributions, respectively. The motion argued that the undisputed material facts established that Coastal Palms systematically excluded Suncoast-collected revenues from its GRR calculations in violation of the plain language of FLA Sections 4.1 and 4.2. Verimark\'s motion was supported by extensive record evidence, including the Suncoast bank records produced pursuant to the Court\'s October 28, 2022 order, Randall Brecker\'s deposition testimony acknowledging the Suncoast revenue-collection arrangement, and Dr. Kettlewell\'s forensic analysis demonstrating the magnitude of the underreporting.

On October 13, 2023, Coastal Palms filed its Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment on all counts of Verimark\'s Complaint and on its own Counterclaim. Coastal Palms argued that the FLA\'s definition of GRR was ambiguous as to whether revenues collected by an affiliated management company (as opposed to the franchisee itself) were properly included, and that Verimark\'s course-of-dealing over nine years of franchise operations --- during which Verimark allegedly knew or should have known about Suncoast\'s role --- constituted waiver or estoppel.

Response briefs were filed on November 17, 2023, and reply briefs on December 8, 2023. Oral argument was held before Judge Calloway on January 19, 2024. Both Priya Anand and Nathan Whitfield III argued the motions. The argument lasted approximately three hours, with the Court asking pointed questions of both sides regarding the FLA\'s GRR definition, the relevance of Suncoast\'s corporate structure, and the applicability of the waiver and estoppel defenses.

On **February 9, 2024**, the Court issued its Order on the cross-motions. The ruling was strongly favorable to Verimark:

> • The Court **granted** Verimark\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on Counts I and II, finding as a matter of law that Coastal Palms\' exclusion of Suncoast-collected revenues from GRR constituted a material breach of Sections 4.1 and 4.2 of each FLA. The Court held that the FLA\'s definition of \"Gross Room Revenue\" --- encompassing \"all revenue derived from or in connection with the rental of guest rooms at the Hotel, regardless of the method of payment, source of booking, or identity of the collecting entity\" --- was unambiguous and clearly encompassed revenues collected by Suncoast on behalf of the franchised properties.
>
> • The Court **denied** Coastal Palms\' Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment in its entirety. The Court rejected the ambiguity defense, the waiver defense (finding that Verimark\'s failure discover the scheme earlier did not constitute knowing acquiescence), and the estoppel defense (finding insufficient evidence of any affirmative representation by Verimark that Suncoast revenues need not be reported).
>
> • The Court **deferred** the determination of damages on Counts I and II to trial, noting that genuine issues of material fact remained regarding the precise calculation of underreported GRR and the applicability of the FLA\'s late-payment interest and liquidated-damages provisions.
>
> • The Court **continued** the trial from February 2024 to May 2024 to allow the parties adequate time to prepare for the damages trial and to explore settlement.

On February 23, 2024, following the summary judgment ruling, the parties agreed to participate in mediation before the Honorable Patricia Everwood (Ret.).

**[D. Significance of Summary Judgment Ruling for Settlement]{.underline}**

The Court\'s February 9, 2024 Order fundamentally altered the litigation landscape and provides Verimark with substantial leverage entering mediation. Several aspects of the ruling are particularly significant:

First, **liability has been established as a matter of law on the two principal counts**. Coastal Palms can no longer contest that it breached the FLAs by excluding Suncoast revenues from GRR. The only remaining issue on Counts I and II is the amount of damages --- a question that, while contested, is bounded by quantifiable financial data.

Second, the Court **explicitly rejected Coastal Palms\' \"ambiguity\" defense** regarding the GRR definition. This was Coastal Palms\' primary defense theory throughout the litigation, and its elimination removes the single most significant obstacle to Verimark\'s recovery. It also substantially undermines the foundation of Professor Hargrove\'s expert opinion, which was predicated on a narrower interpretation of GRR that the Court has now rejected.

Third, the denial of Coastal Palms\' cross-motion, including on its counterclaim, signals that the Court views Coastal Palms\' positions skeptically. While the counterclaim remains pending, Coastal Palms failed to obtain summary judgment even on its own affirmative claims, suggesting the counterclaim faces significant headwinds at trial.

The remaining issues for trial include: (i) the precise quantification of damages on Counts I and II; (ii) liability and damages on Counts III through X, which present additional complexity and some litigation risk; and (iii) Coastal Palms\' counterclaim. However, the core liability finding on the two principal counts means that Coastal Palms now faces a near-certain adverse monetary judgment, with the question being only how large that judgment will be. This dynamic should create meaningful pressure on Coastal Palms to settle on terms favorable to Verimark.

**[III. DAMAGES ANALYSIS]{.underline}**

**[A. Verimark\'s Claimed Damages --- Full Model]{.underline}**

Verimark\'s total claimed damages in this action amount to approximately \$150 million. This figure is composed of the following elements, each of which is supported by the forensic analysis of Dr. Sharon Kettlewell and the franchise-compliance audit of Thornbury & Associates CPAs LLP:

1\. **Underreported Gross Room Revenue (2013--2021):** The Thornbury/Kettlewell forensic estimate, based on analysis of Suncoast bank records, OTA reconciliations, PMS data, and property-level financial records across all 22 Coastal Palms properties, determined that total underreported GRR for the 2013--2021 period was approximately **\$197.8 million**. This figure represents the difference between the GRR that Coastal Palms reported to Verimark and the actual GRR that should have been reported under the FLA definitions.

2\. **Underpaid Royalties (5% of \$197.8 million):** Under Section 4.1 of each FLA, Coastal Palms was required to pay Verimark a continuing royalty equal to 5% of monthly GRR. Applied to the underreported GRR of \$197.8 million, the resulting underpayment of royalties totals **\$9.89 million**.

3\. **Underpaid Marketing-Fund Contributions (2.5% of \$197.8 million):** Under Section 4.2 of each FLA, Coastal Palms was required to contribute 2.5% of monthly GRR to Verimark\'s national marketing fund. Applied to the underreported GRR, the underpayment of marketing-fund contributions totals **\$4.945 million**.

4\. **Underpaid Technology Fees:** Separate from the GRR-based fees, Section 4.3 of each FLA requires the franchisee to pay a per-room technology fee of \$12.50 per room per month to support Verimark\'s central reservation system, property-management system integration, and guest-loyalty platform. The Thornbury audit identified that Coastal Palms added a total of 214 rooms across 4 properties without providing the required written notice to Verimark, and without paying the corresponding technology fees. Based on 214 rooms at \$12.50 per room per month for an average of 47 months of non-payment per room, the underpaid technology fees total **\$1.26 million**.

5\. **Subtotal of Direct Underpayments:** \$9.89 million + \$4.945 million + \$1.26 million = **\$16.095 million**.

6\. **Contractual Late-Payment Interest (FLA Section 4.6):** Each FLA provides that any amounts not paid when due shall bear interest at a rate of 1.5% per month, compounded monthly. Dr. Kettlewell\'s model calculates interest on each monthly underpayment from the date due through a projected judgment date of June 30, 2024. The resulting late-payment interest totals approximately **\$28.4 million**. This figure reflects the compounding effect over an extended period --- some underpayments date back to 2013, representing over 10 years of accrued interest.

7\. **Liquidated Damages (FLA Section 15.3):** Upon termination of an FLA for material breach, Section 15.3 provides for liquidated damages equal to three times the trailing-twelve-month royalties for the affected property. Applied across all 22 properties using corrected (actual) GRR figures for the most recent trailing twelve months, the liquidated-damages claim totals approximately **\$105.5 million**. This figure varies by property based on each property\'s actual revenue level.

8\. **Grand Total --- Claimed Damages:** Approximately **\$150 million** (\$16.095 million in direct underpayments + \$28.4 million in contractual interest + \$105.5 million in liquidated damages).

It is important to note that the \$150 million figure represents the maximum amount Verimark could potentially recover under its contract claims. The actual recovery is subject to significant uncertainties, as discussed in Section III.D below.

**[B. Dr. Sharon Kettlewell\'s Expert Report (Ridgeline Forensic Advisory LLC)]{.underline}**

Dr. Sharon Kettlewell, a forensic accounting expert and managing director of Ridgeline Forensic Advisory LLC, was retained to quantify the damages resulting from Coastal Palms\' underreporting scheme. Dr. Kettlewell served her initial expert report on April 14, 2023, and her rebuttal report on June 9, 2023. She was deposed on June 26, 2023. Dr. Kettlewell\'s opinions are well-supported, methodologically sound, and have been effectively validated by the Court\'s summary judgment ruling.

Dr. Kettlewell\'s analysis identified and documented the specific revenue-diversion scheme employed by Coastal Palms. The scheme operated as follows: Suncoast Room Management Inc., a Florida corporation whose president is Randall Brecker (who simultaneously serves as 60% equity holder and managing member of Coastal Palms), collected revenues from three categories of bookings that were diverted outside of the Verimark-integrated reporting system:

> • **Walk-in guests:** Cash and credit-card payments from guests who arrived at the properties without advance reservations were processed through Suncoast\'s merchant accounts rather than through the Verimark-integrated PMS;
>
> • **Corporate-direct contracts:** Coastal Palms maintained corporate rate agreements with approximately 47 regional businesses through Suncoast, with payments flowing directly to Suncoast\'s accounts; and
>
> • **gulfcoastrooms.com website bookings:** Suncoast operated a direct-booking website, gulfcoastrooms.com, which marketed and accepted reservations for Coastal Palms properties outside of Verimark\'s central reservation system.

Under this arrangement, Suncoast collected the revenues from these sources, retained a 12% \"management fee,\" and remitted the remaining balance to property-level limited liability companies --- specifically Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC and Savannah Lodging Partners LLC --- rather than reporting any of these amounts through the Verimark franchise reporting system. Neither Suncoast\'s collections nor the 12% management fee were reported as GRR to Verimark.

In addition to the Suncoast diversion scheme, Dr. Kettlewell identified a second category of underreporting involving OTA channels. Coastal Palms classified net-rate OTA payments (from platforms such as Aldermere Technologies, Bramwell Holdings, and Drayton Software) as \"commissions receivable\" and netted the OTA commissions against GRR, reporting only the net amount to Verimark. This practice violated Section 4.1\'s definition of GRR, which requires reporting on a gross basis --- that is, the total amount paid by the guest, not the net amount received after commission deductions.

Dr. Kettlewell\'s quantification of underreported GRR was based on a comprehensive reconstruction methodology that drew upon the following data sources, which were obtained through the litigation discovery process:

> • Suncoast bank statements (all accounts, 2013--2021), produced pursuant to the Court\'s October 28, 2022 order;
>
> • OTA settlement and reconciliation statements from Hollowell Industries, Ridgeway & Co., and other OTA platforms;
>
> • PMS data exports from the Opera and Choice Advantage systems used at various Coastal Palms properties;
>
> • Property-level general ledger and financial statement data from the Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC and Savannah Lodging Partners LLC entities; and
>
> • Tax returns, bank deposit records, and merchant-processing statements.

The key findings of Dr. Kettlewell\'s analysis include:

> • **FY 2021 reported GRR:** \$112.4 million across 22 properties;
>
> • **FY 2021 estimated true GRR:** \$145.6 million;
>
> • **FY 2021 underreported GRR:** \$33.2 million (approximately 29.5% of reported GRR);
>
> • **Underreporting percentage range:** 22% to 31%, varying by property and year, with the highest underreporting rates at the Fort Myers and Savannah properties where corporate-direct contracts and gulfcoastrooms.com bookings were most prevalent;
>

**[SETTLEMENT TERM SHEET]{.underline}**

**NON-BINDING EXCEPT AS SET FORTH IN SECTIONS 12 AND 13 BELOW**

March 22, 2024

In connection with *Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC et al.*, Case No. 1021-00006, Circuit Court of the 17th Judicial Circuit in and for Broward County, Florida.

**[PREAMBLE AND RECITALS]{.underline}**

This Settlement Term Sheet (this \"Term Sheet\") sets forth the principal terms upon which the Parties (as defined below) intend to resolve the above-captioned action and all related claims, counterclaims, cross-claims, and third-party claims arising therefrom or related thereto.

The Parties to this Term Sheet are:

**Verimark Hospitality Group Inc.** (\"Verimark\" or \"VHG\"), a corporation duly organized and existing under the laws of the State of Delaware, publicly traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol VHMK, with its principal executive offices located at 2400 East Las Olas Boulevard, Suite 3100, Fort Lauderdale, Florida 33301, acting by and through its duly authorized officer and its counsel of record, Calderwood & Harkness LLP (Priya Anand, Responsible Partner);

**Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC** (\"Coastal Palms\" or \"CPFH\"), a limited liability company organized and existing under the laws of the State of Florida, with its principal offices located at 9500 Gulf Shore Drive, Suite 450, Naples, Florida 34108, acting by and through its Managing Member and its counsel of record, Whitfield, Barrow & Crane LLP (Nathan Whitfield III, Senior Partner);

**Randall \"Randy\" Brecker** (\"Brecker\"), individually, a resident of the State of Florida, in his capacity as Managing Member and sixty percent (60%) equity holder of Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC and in his capacity as President of Suncoast Room Management Inc., a Florida corporation; and

**Nolan Prescott** (\"Prescott\"), individually, a resident of the State of Florida, in his capacity as a Member and twenty-five percent (25%) equity holder of Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC.

(Each, a \"Party\" and collectively, the \"Parties.\")

**WHEREAS**, the Litigation (as defined herein) arises from Verimark\'s claims that Coastal Palms, under the direction and control of Brecker and Prescott, engaged in systematic and deliberate underreporting of Gross Room Revenue (\"GRR\") across twenty-two (22) franchised hotel properties --- consisting of eighteen (18) Verimark Suites--branded properties and four (4) Verimark Select--branded properties --- over the period from January 1, 2013 through December 31, 2021, resulting in alleged material underpayment of royalties, marketing-fund contributions, and technology fees owed to Verimark under the individual Franchise License Agreements (\"FLAs\") governing each such property;

**WHEREAS**, Verimark\'s Complaint, as amended, asserts claims for breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, unjust enrichment, fraudulent concealment, and violations of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, Chapter 501, Part II, Florida Statutes, and seeks damages in excess of \$125,000,000, together with attorneys\' fees, costs, pre-judgment interest, and equitable relief;

**WHEREAS**, Coastal Palms filed a Counterclaim on April 18, 2022, in the amount of Twelve Million Dollars (\$12,000,000), alleging that Verimark committed brand-standard violations by failing to maintain adequate reservation-system infrastructure, and further alleging that Verimark engaged in systematic over-billing of technology fees across all twenty-two (22) franchised properties;

**WHEREAS**, on February 9, 2024, the Court (Honorable Richard M. Calloway, Circuit Judge) entered an Order granting Verimark\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on Count I (Breach of Contract --- Royalties) and Count II (Breach of Contract --- Marketing Fund), finding as a matter of law that Coastal Palms\' exclusion of revenues collected by and through Suncoast Room Management Inc. from the calculation of Gross Room Revenue constituted a material breach of Sections 4.1 and 4.2 of the FLAs, with the determination of damages deferred to trial;

**WHEREAS**, the Parties participated in a two-day mediation on March 14--15, 2024, before the Honorable Patricia Everwood (Ret.) at Everwood Dispute Resolution PLLC, Coral Gables, Florida, and reached a tentative agreement on the principal settlement terms memorialized herein; and

**WHEREAS**, except as expressly provided in Section 12 (Exclusivity) and Section 13 (Confidentiality) below, this Term Sheet is non-binding and is intended solely to facilitate the negotiation and execution of a definitive Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release (the \"Definitive Agreement\").

**NOW, THEREFORE**, in consideration of the foregoing recitals and the mutual covenants and agreements contained herein, and for other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, the Parties set forth the following principal settlement terms:

**[SECTION 1: SETTLEMENT AMOUNT]{.underline}**

1.1 **Total Settlement Consideration.** The total settlement consideration shall be Eighty-Seven Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$87,500,000) (the \"Settlement Amount\"). The Settlement Amount represents a negotiated compromise of the Parties\' respective claims and counterclaims and does not constitute an admission of liability by any Party.

1.2 **Cash Payment at Closing.** Twenty-Five Million Dollars (\$25,000,000) of the Settlement Amount shall be payable on the Closing Date (as defined in Section 2 below) by wire transfer of immediately available funds to an account designated in writing by Verimark no fewer than five (5) business days prior to the Closing Date (the \"Cash Payment at Closing\"). The Cash Payment at Closing shall be sourced from the escrow account currently maintained by Coastal Palms at Ironclad National Bank, Account No. \[to be provided\], and shall be initiated and completed on the Closing Date.

1.3 **Structured Payments.** The remaining Sixty-Two Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$62,500,000) of the Settlement Amount shall be payable in eight (8) equal semi-annual installments of Seven Million Eight Hundred Twelve Thousand Five Hundred Dollars (\$7,812,500) each (each, a \"Structured Payment\"), in accordance with the following payment schedule:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Installment No.**     **Due Date**            **Principal Amount**
  ----------------------- ----------------------- -----------------------
  1                       October 22, 2024        \$7,812,500

  2                       April 22, 2025          \$7,812,500

  3                       October 22, 2025        \$7,812,500

  4                       April 22, 2026          \$7,812,500

  5                       October 22, 2026        \$7,812,500

  6                       April 22, 2027          \$7,812,500

  7                       October 22, 2027        \$7,812,500

  8                       April 22, 2028          \$7,812,500

                          **Total**               **\$62,500,000**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The first Structured Payment shall be due and payable on October 22, 2024, which is six (6) months after the anticipated Closing Date. Each subsequent Structured Payment shall be due and payable on the 22nd day of each successive six-month period thereafter, with the final Structured Payment due on April 22, 2028.

1.4 **Interest.** Simple interest shall accrue on the outstanding unpaid principal balance of the Structured Payments at a rate of six and one-half percent (6.5%) per annum (the \"Contract Rate\"), calculated from the Closing Date. Interest shall be payable concurrently with each Structured Payment. For the avoidance of doubt, interest shall be calculated on a 365-day year basis, and each interest payment shall cover the six-month period immediately preceding the applicable Structured Payment due date. The interest component of each payment shall be in addition to, and not inclusive of, the principal installment amount set forth in the schedule above.

1.5 **Method of Payment.** All payments of principal and interest shall be made by wire transfer of immediately available funds to an account or accounts designated by Verimark in writing. Verimark shall provide wiring instructions to Coastal Palms no fewer than ten (10) business days prior to the Closing Date, and such wiring instructions shall remain in effect for all subsequent Structured Payments unless Verimark provides updated instructions in writing at least five (5) business days prior to any payment due date.

1.6 **Joint and Several Liability.** All payment obligations under this Section 1, including the Cash Payment at Closing, the Structured Payments, and all accrued interest thereon, shall be the joint and several obligation of (a) Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC, (b) Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC, a Florida limited liability company and affiliate of Coastal Palms, (c) Savannah Lodging Partners LLC, a Georgia limited liability company and affiliate of Coastal Palms, and (d) Suncoast Room Management Inc., a Florida corporation. The joint and several liability of the foregoing entities shall be set forth in detail in the Definitive Agreement and shall be in addition to the personal guaranties described in Section 3 below.

**[SECTION 2: CLOSING DATE]{.underline}**

2.1 **Closing Date.** The \"Closing Date\" shall be the date on which the Definitive Agreement is fully executed and delivered by all Parties. The Parties shall use their respective best efforts to cause the Closing Date to occur on or before April 22, 2024, which is thirty (30) calendar days from the date of this Term Sheet.

2.2 **Exchange of Closing Deliverables.** On or before the Closing Date, all closing deliverables identified in Section 10 below shall be exchanged simultaneously, or in such order as the Parties may agree. No closing deliverable shall be deemed effective until all closing deliverables have been exchanged and the Cash Payment at Closing has been received by Verimark in immediately available funds.

2.3 **Extension of Closing Date.** The Closing Date may be extended by mutual written agreement of the Parties, provided that in no event shall the Closing Date be extended beyond the expiration of the Exclusivity Period (as defined in Section 12 below) without the prior written consent of all Parties.

**[SECTION 3: SECURITY FOR STRUCTURED PAYMENTS]{.underline}**

3.1 **First-Priority Lien on Collateral Properties.** As security for the full and timely payment of all Structured Payments and interest thereon, Coastal Palms shall grant to Verimark a first-priority security interest and lien on eight (8) hotel properties that are currently unencumbered by any mortgage, deed of trust, or other lien (collectively, the \"Collateral Properties\"). The Collateral Properties have an aggregate appraised value of approximately Seventy-One Million Two Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$71,200,000), based on appraisals conducted within the twelve (12) months preceding the date of this Term Sheet. The specific identity, address, legal description, and appraised value of each Collateral Property shall be set forth in a schedule to be attached as an exhibit to the Definitive Agreement.

3.2 **Perfection of Security Interest.** The security interest in the Collateral Properties shall be perfected by (a) the filing of a UCC-1 Financing Statement with the Florida Secured Transaction Registry, and (b) as applicable to each Collateral Property, the recordation of a mortgage or deed of trust in the official records of the county in which such Collateral Property is situated. All filing fees, recording fees, documentary stamp taxes, and related costs associated with the perfection of Verimark\'s security interest shall be borne by Coastal Palms. Coastal Palms shall cooperate fully with Verimark and its counsel in connection with the preparation, execution, and filing of all instruments and documents necessary or desirable to perfect and maintain Verimark\'s first-priority security interest in the Collateral Properties.

3.3 **Personal Guaranties.** As additional security for the full and timely payment of all obligations under the Definitive Agreement, each of Randall Brecker and Nolan Prescott shall execute and deliver to Verimark a personal, unconditional, and irrevocable guaranty of all payment obligations of Coastal Palms and the other jointly and severally liable entities under the Definitive Agreement (each, a \"Personal Guaranty\" and collectively, the \"Personal Guaranties\"). The form, scope, and specific terms of the Personal Guaranties, including any limitations on liability, subordination provisions, and notice requirements, shall be negotiated in good faith and set forth in the Definitive Agreement or in a separate guaranty agreement attached thereto as an exhibit.

3.4 **Acknowledgment by Ironclad National Bank.** Coastal Palms shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain, on or before the Closing Date, a written acknowledgment and consent from Ironclad National Bank (attention: Devon Schultz, Senior Vice President, Commercial Real Estate Lending) regarding Verimark\'s security interest and lien position on the Collateral Properties. The Parties acknowledge that Ironclad National Bank currently holds first-lien mortgage loans on eighteen (18) of the twenty-two (22) hotel properties operated by Coastal Palms, with an aggregate outstanding principal balance of approximately Ninety-Four Million Dollars (\$94,000,000); however, the eight (8) Collateral Properties identified for purposes of this Section 3 are unencumbered by any Ironclad National Bank liens. The acknowledgment and consent of Ironclad National Bank is being sought to confirm the bank\'s awareness of, and non-objection to, Verimark\'s lien position on the Collateral Properties and to address any potential cross-collateralization or cross-default provisions that may exist in Coastal Palms\' loan agreements with Ironclad National Bank. The failure to obtain such acknowledgment and consent shall not, by itself, constitute a condition to closing, unless the Parties otherwise agree in the Definitive Agreement.

**[SECTION 4: ACCELERATION AND DEFAULT]{.underline}**

4.1 **Events of Default.** An \"Event of Default\" shall include, without limitation, the occurrence of any of the following:

> \(a\) The failure by Coastal Palms, or any jointly and severally liable entity, to make any Structured Payment or interest payment within fifteen (15) calendar days of the applicable due date;
>
> \(b\) The breach of any material term, covenant, representation, or warranty contained in the Definitive Agreement, the Personal Guaranties, the security instruments, or the New FLAs (as defined in Section 6 below), subject to a reasonable cure period to be specified in the Definitive Agreement (anticipated to be thirty (30) days from written notice of such breach for non-monetary defaults);
>
> \(c\) The filing by or against Coastal Palms, any affiliate of Coastal Palms (including Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC, Savannah Lodging Partners LLC, and Suncoast Room Management Inc.), or any guarantor (including Randall Brecker and Nolan Prescott) of a voluntary or involuntary petition under Title 11 of the United States Code (the Bankruptcy Code), or any state-law insolvency proceeding, assignment for the benefit of creditors, or appointment of a receiver, trustee, or custodian for all or substantially all of such Party\'s assets;
>
> \(d\) Any material adverse change in the condition, value, or encumbrance status of the Collateral Properties that materially impairs Verimark\'s security interest therein, including without limitation the imposition of any lien, encumbrance, or claim on the Collateral Properties without Verimark\'s prior written consent; and
>
> \(e\) Any other events of default as the Parties may agree upon in the Definitive Agreement.

4.2 **Acceleration.** Upon the occurrence and during the continuance of an Event of Default, Verimark shall have the right, in its sole discretion, upon written notice to Coastal Palms and the guarantors, to accelerate all remaining Structured Payments, together with all accrued and unpaid interest thereon, which amounts shall thereupon become immediately due and payable in full, without presentment, demand, protest, or further notice of any kind, all of which are hereby expressly waived to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law.

4.3 **Default Interest Rate.** Upon the occurrence of an Event of Default, the interest rate applicable to all outstanding obligations shall increase to a default rate to be specified in the Definitive Agreement (anticipated to be the lesser of (i) the Contract Rate plus four percent (4%) per annum, or (ii) the maximum rate permitted by applicable Florida law).

4.4 **Additional Remedies.** In addition to acceleration, Verimark shall be entitled to exercise all rights and remedies available to it under the Definitive Agreement, the security instruments, applicable law (including Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code), and equity, including without limitation foreclosure on the Collateral Properties, enforcement of the Personal Guaranties, and recovery of all reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs incurred in connection with the enforcement of its rights. All remedies shall be cumulative and not exclusive.

**[SECTION 5: FRANCHISE SURRENDER]{.underline}**

5.1 **Surrendered Properties.** Coastal Palms shall surrender its franchise rights with respect to fourteen (14) of the twenty-two (22) hotel properties currently operated under the Verimark Suites and Verimark Select brands (collectively, the \"Surrendered Properties\"). The Surrendered Properties are located in the following markets:

> \(a\) Sarasota, Florida --- three (3) properties;
>
> \(b\) Fort Myers, Florida --- four (4) properties;
>
> \(c\) Jacksonville, Florida --- two (2) properties;
>
> \(d\) Savannah, Georgia --- three (3) properties; and
>
> \(e\) Brunswick, Georgia --- two (2) properties.

The specific name, address, and FLA reference number for each Surrendered Property shall be set forth in a schedule to be attached as an exhibit to the Definitive Agreement.

5.2 **Termination of FLAs.** All Franchise License Agreements associated with the Surrendered Properties shall be terminated effective as of the Closing Date, provided that Coastal Palms\' de-identification obligations under Section 5.3 below shall survive such termination and remain in full force and effect during the De-Identification Period.

5.3 **De-Identification Obligations.** Coastal Palms shall, at its sole cost and expense, complete the de-identification of all Surrendered Properties within one hundred twenty (120) calendar days of the Closing Date (the \"De-Identification Period\"). Assuming a Closing Date of April 22, 2024, the deadline for completion of de-identification shall be August 20, 2024. De-identification shall include, without limitation:

> \(a\) The removal of all Verimark branding, including all exterior and interior signage bearing the \"Verimark Suites\" and \"Verimark Select\" names, logos, and trade dress;
>
> \(b\) The removal or disabling of all proprietary Verimark systems, including but not limited to reservation systems, property management system interfaces, guest loyalty program terminals, and revenue-management software;
>
> \(c\) The removal of all Verimark trade dress, including branded linens, amenity packages, room collateral, in-room directories, key cards, and uniforms bearing the Verimark name, logo, or any related marks;
>
> \(d\) The de-listing of all Surrendered Properties from Verimark\'s online booking platforms, mobile applications, and third-party distribution channels operating under Verimark\'s brand umbrella; and
>
> \(e\) Such other de-identification steps as Verimark may reasonably require consistent with its standard franchise termination procedures.

5.4 **Consequences of Failure to De-Identify.** The specific consequences of Coastal Palms\' failure to complete de-identification of any Surrendered Property within the De-Identification Period, including liquidated damages, injunctive relief, and Verimark\'s right to enter the property to effect de-identification at Coastal Palms\' expense, shall be set forth in the Definitive Agreement.

**[SECTION 6: RETAINED PROPERTIES AND ENHANCED AUDIT PROTOCOL]{.underline}**

6.1 **Retained Properties.** Coastal Palms shall retain its franchise rights with respect to eight (8) hotel properties (the \"Retained Properties\"), located in the following markets:

> \(a\) Naples, Florida --- four (4) properties;
>
> \(b\) Marco Island, Florida --- two (2) properties; and
>
> \(c\) Tampa, Florida --- two (2) properties.

The specific name, address, and room count for each Retained Property shall be set forth in a schedule to be attached as an exhibit to the Definitive Agreement.

6.2 **New Franchise License Agreements.** On the Closing Date, Coastal Palms and Verimark shall execute new Franchise License Agreements for each of the eight (8) Retained Properties (collectively, the \"New FLAs\"). Each New FLA shall have an initial term of ten (10) years commencing on the Closing Date and shall incorporate all standard terms and conditions of Verimark\'s then-current form Franchise License Agreement, as supplemented by the enhanced provisions described in Sections 6.3 through 6.6 below.

6.3 **Quarterly Audit Rights.** For a period of five (5) years from the Closing Date (the \"Enhanced Audit Period\"), Verimark and its duly authorized designees (including independent auditors, forensic accountants, and revenue-assurance consultants) shall have the right to conduct quarterly audits of Gross Room Revenue at each Retained Property. This enhanced audit frequency replaces the standard annual audit right provided under Verimark\'s form FLA and is being implemented in light of the revenue-reporting deficiencies that gave rise to the Litigation. Coastal Palms shall make available all books, records, documents, and electronic data reasonably requested by Verimark or its designees in connection with each quarterly audit, and shall provide Verimark\'s auditors with reasonable access to each Retained Property and its on-site personnel during normal business hours upon not fewer than five (5) business days\' prior written notice. Following the expiration of the Enhanced Audit Period, audit rights shall revert to the standard annual frequency provided under the New FLAs.

6.4 **Real-Time Point-of-Sale Integration.** Coastal Palms shall implement and maintain real-time point-of-sale (\"POS\") integration with Verimark\'s centralized revenue-management system (\"VeriConnect RMS\") at each Retained Property within ninety (90) calendar days of the Closing Date. Such integration shall enable Verimark to monitor and verify Gross Room Revenue data on a continuous, real-time basis, and shall include connectivity with all front-desk property management systems, online booking engines, and third-party channel managers utilized at each Retained Property. Coastal Palms shall bear all costs associated with the initial implementation and ongoing maintenance of the POS integration, including hardware, software licensing, connectivity, and training expenses.

6.5 **Audit Cost Allocation.** Coastal Palms shall bear all costs and expenses associated with the quarterly audits during the initial five-year Enhanced Audit Period, regardless of the findings of any such audit. Such costs shall include, without limitation, the fees and expenses of independent auditors and forensic accountants engaged by Verimark, travel and lodging expenses, and data extraction and analysis costs. This allocation of audit costs differs from Verimark\'s standard FLA, under which audit costs are borne by the franchisor unless the audit reveals an underreporting variance of five percent (5%) or more, in which case such costs are charged to the franchisee.

6.6 **Standard Economic Terms.** All other economic terms of the New FLAs shall be consistent with Verimark\'s standard form Franchise License Agreement, including:

> \(a\) Royalty fee: five percent (5%) of Gross Room Revenue;
>
> \(b\) Marketing-fund contribution: two and one-half percent (2.5%) of Gross Room Revenue; and
>
> \(c\) Technology fee: Twelve Dollars and Fifty Cents (\$12.50) per room per month.

6.7 **Form of New FLAs.** The form of New FLA, incorporating the enhanced provisions described in this Section 6, shall be attached as an exhibit to the Definitive Agreement and shall be executed simultaneously with the Definitive Agreement on the Closing Date.

**[SECTION 7: MUTUAL RELEASE]{.underline}**

7.1 **Scope of Mutual Release.** Effective as of the Closing Date, each Party, on behalf of itself and its respective affiliates, subsidiaries, parent companies, predecessors, successors, assigns, officers, directors, members, managers, employees, agents, representatives, attorneys, heirs, executors, administrators, and insurers, shall release and forever discharge each other Party and such other Party\'s respective affiliates, subsidiaries, parent companies, predecessors, successors, assigns, officers, directors, members, managers, employees, agents, representatives, attorneys, heirs, executors, administrators, and insurers, from any and all claims, counterclaims, demands, actions, causes of action, suits, debts, dues, sums of money, accounts, reckonings, bonds, bills, covenants, contracts, controversies, agreements, promises, variances, trespasses, damages, judgments, executions, liabilities, and obligations of every kind and nature whatsoever, whether known or unknown, suspected or unsuspected, contingent or matured, liquidated or unliquidated, at law or in equity, arising from or related to the FLAs, the Litigation (Case No. 1021-00006), and the subject matter thereof, from the beginning of time through and including the Closing Date.

## Confidentiality Notice {#slide-1}

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION AND ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

Prepared by Calderwood & Harkness LLP for the Board Audit Committee of Quorum Insurance Holdings Corp.

Matter No. 1025-00005

March 24, 2026

## Executive Summary {#slide-2}

Pinnacle Atlantic Reinsurance Ltd. has issued a pre-suit demand seeking return of \$78.4M in recoverables plus \$12.6M interest --- total demand of \$91.0M

Dispute concerns cessions under Treaty No. PA-QCS-2019-EXL-0044 (2019 aggregate excess-of-loss treaty) between QC&S (cedent) and Pinnacle Atlantic (reinsurer)

Treaty years at issue: TY 2022 (\$69.7M ceded) and TY 2023 (\$8.7M ceded)

Pre-suit demand letter dated February 14, 2026, from Hargrove, Fitch & Calloway LLP

Calderwood & Harkness retained March 2, 2026, following Audit Committee authorization on February 24, 2026

QC&S has strong defenses on all four grounds; recommended strategy: enforce treaty arbitration, propose mediation, prepare robust pre-litigation posture

## Parties and Key Personnel {#slide-3}

Cedent: Quorum Casualty & Surety Company --- NY-domiciled (NAIC 24891); A.M. Ridgeway: A (Excellent), Stable; statutory surplus \$1.42B (Dec. 31, 2025)

Reinsurer: Pinnacle Atlantic Reinsurance Ltd. --- Bermuda Class 4 insurer; U.S. office at 1285 Avenue of the Americas, New York

Opposing counsel: Hargrove, Fitch & Calloway LLP (Nathaniel R. Calloway III, Lead Partner; Priya Subramanian, Senior Associate)

QIH counsel: Calderwood & Harkness LLP (Carmichael, Morano, Park, Nakamura)

Key QIH personnel: Rachel Sondergaard (GC), Tobias Engström (SVP, Reinsurance & Capital Markets), Diana Kessler-Hoff (VP, Claims & Reinsurance Recoveries)

Broker: Broadreach Intermediaries Inc. (Jamie Castellano); Consulting Actuaries: Velthorn Actuarial Advisors LLC (Dr. Stephen Tanaka, FCAS, MAAA)

## Treaty Overview --- PA-QCS-2019-EXL-0044 {#slide-4}

Type: Aggregate excess-of-loss reinsurance treaty --- casualty lines (CGL, excess/umbrella, professional liability)

Inception: July 1, 2019; original 5-year term through June 30, 2024; extended through June 30, 2026

Retention: \$120M per treaty year in aggregate net incurred losses; Cession limit: \$200M per treaty year (\$120M--\$320M)

Premium: Provisional rate of 42% of ceded earned premium; slide-scale adjustment (min 35%, max 52%)

Governing law: New York; Arbitration: Article 22 --- three-member panel, ARIAS-U.S. Rules, seated in New York

Intermediary: Broadreach Intermediaries Inc. (Article 9)

Pinnacle Atlantic issued non-renewal notice October 1, 2025; treaty lapses June 30, 2026

## Disputed Cessions --- Financial Breakdown {#slide-5}

TY 2022: QC&S aggregate net incurred loss of \$189.7M − \$120.0M retention = \$69.7M ceded

TY 2023: QC&S aggregate net incurred loss of \$128.7M − \$120.0M retention = \$8.7M ceded

Total ceded (and billed/paid): \$78.4M (\$69.7M + \$8.7M)

Pinnacle Atlantic paid the full \$78.4M across seven billing installments (October 2022 -- March 2024)

Pinnacle Atlantic now demands return of \$78.4M + \$12.6M interest = \$91.0M total

Interest calculated at \~8% per annum, approximately 24-month average duration

## Pinnacle Atlantic\'s Four Grounds for Dispute {#slide-6}

1. Late Notice (Article 7): Alleges 14-month, 7-day delay in noticing the Meridian Docks mass tort cluster (first reserve March 15, 2021; notice May 22, 2022)

2. IBNR Misallocation (Article 5): Alleges \$22.3M in IBNR reserve strengthening was improperly allocated to TY 2022 instead of TY 2021

3. Follow-the-Fortunes (Article 11): Challenges \$34.5M Veridian Financial Services E&O cluster settlement as not in the ordinary course

4. Premium Underreporting (Article 3): Alleges \$6.8M underreported TY 2022 ceded earned premium; \$2.856M premium underpayment

## QC&S Defenses --- Late Notice (Ground 1) {#slide-7}

Article 7 has a \$1M individual claim reporting threshold; Meridian Docks claims were individually below this threshold until Q1 2022 reserve increases

QC&S provided prompt notice once the aggregate reserve crossed the treaty reporting threshold --- notice given May 22, 2022, via Broadreach

NY law applies a prejudice-based standard: Pinnacle Atlantic must show actual prejudice from any delay

Pinnacle Atlantic has not articulated any specific prejudice arising from the timing of notice

QC&S claims handling procedures and reserving practices were consistent with industry norms

## QC&S Defenses --- IBNR Allocation (Ground 2) {#slide-8}

Velthorn Actuarial Advisors\' analysis supports allocation to accident-year 2022 based on development factors that crystallized during TY 2022

Treaty Article 5.2 definition of \'losses incurred\' supports QC&S\'s allocation methodology

If Pinnacle Atlantic\'s reallocation were accepted: TY 2022 ceded loss drops from \$69.7M to \$47.4M

TY 2021 aggregate was \$104.6M (below \$120M retention); adding \$22.3M yields \$126.9M --- only \$6.9M cession in an undisputed treaty year

Actuarial standards of practice support Velthorn\'s methodology; Dr. Stephen Tanaka prepared actuarial certificates

Net effect of reallocation dispute: potential \$22.3M reduction, not full invalidation

## QC&S Defenses --- Follow-the-Fortunes / Veridian Settlement (Ground 3) {#slide-9}

Follow-the-fortunes doctrine under NY law provides broad deference to a cedent\'s good-faith claims handling and settlement decisions

Reinsurer can overcome the doctrine only by showing bad faith, fraud, or gross negligence --- a very high bar

Veridian \$34.5M settlement resulted from genuine claims evaluation; QC&S retained \$26.1M net --- significant \'skin in the game\'

Pinnacle Atlantic\'s allegation that settlements were inflated to breach the retention is speculative and unsupported

QC&S claims file documentation supports the reasonableness of each settlement amount

Only \$8.7M of the Veridian settlement flowed through to the Treaty (TY 2023 cession)

## QC&S Defenses --- Premium Reporting (Ground 4) {#slide-10}

Discrepancy arises from Pinnacle Atlantic\'s improper inclusion of run-off portfolio transfer premiums excluded under Article 3.4

QC&S reported \$38.4M ceded earned premium for TY 2022; Pinnacle Atlantic calculates \$45.2M --- difference of \$6.8M

Even if underreporting were established, alleged shortfall is \$2.856M (\$6.8M × 42%) --- a premium adjustment, not grounds for rescission

Article 3 provides no termination right for premium reporting disputes; any shortfall results in offset or true-up

Slide-scale premium adjustment mechanism (35%--52%) contemplates ongoing reconciliation

## Forum and Procedural Strategy --- Arbitration vs. Litigation {#slide-11}

Treaty Article 22 provides for mandatory arbitration: three-member panel, ARIAS-U.S. Rules, seated in New York

Hargrove, Fitch & Calloway asserts the arbitration clause is inapplicable --- we believe this position lacks merit

NY law and the Federal Arbitration Act strongly favor enforcement of broad arbitration clauses in reinsurance treaties

Recommended: demand arbitration immediately; if suit is filed in NY Commercial Division, move to compel arbitration and stay litigation

Arbitration advantages: industry-expert arbitrators, confidentiality, potentially faster resolution

C&H sent demand to arbitrate on March 18, 2026, and has prepared draft motion to compel

## Additional Strategic Recommendations {#slide-12}

Propose voluntary mediation --- one-day session in New York with a reinsurance-experienced neutral

Mediation proposal sent to HFC on approximately March 25, 2026, without prejudice to arbitration demand

Prepare robust defensive pleadings: verified answer, affirmative defenses, and counterclaim for declaratory judgment

Assert waiver defense: Pinnacle Atlantic paid \$78.4M across 7 installments over 18 months without reservation

Coordinate with Harmon & Whitfield LLP on regulatory issues and Meridian Whitcomb on audit implications

Retain independent actuarial expert and reinsurance industry practices expert

## Exposure Analysis --- Best / Likely / Worst Case {#slide-13}

{"file_path":"response.md","content":"# Largest executed litigation settlement

## Answer

The largest executed settlement identified in the firm’s files is **$87,500,000** (the agreement’s defined principal **“Settlement Amount”**) in ***Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC, et al.***, **Case No. 1021-00006**, Circuit Court of the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit in and for Broward County, Florida.

The executed agreement is dated **April 22, 2024**. It resolves Verimark’s claims arising from Coastal Palms’ alleged systematic underreporting of hotel gross-room revenue and related underpayment of royalties, marketing-fund contributions, and technology fees.

## Documents relied on

1. **Executed settlement agreement:**
   - `documents/matters/1021-00006/Mediation & Settlement/final-settlement-agreement-execution.docx`
   - The agreement identifies the action and parties, defines the “Settlement Amount” as **$87,500,000** in **Section 1.22**, and states in **Section 2.1** that the total settlement amount is $87,500,000.
   - Section 2.1 divides that amount into:
     - **$25,000,000** initial payment at closing; and
     - **$62,500,000** in eight structured principal payments of **$7,812,500** each.
   - The signature pages are dated April 22, 2024. The agreement also includes an exhibit with the payment schedule.

2. **Settlement authority memorandum:**
   - `documents/matters/1021-00006/Mediation & Settlement/settlement-authority-memo.docx`
   - This pre-execution memorandum recommended authority of **$75 million–$95 million** and specifically identified a target settlement of approximately **$87.5 million**, with $25 million at closing and $62.5 million structured. This corroborates the negotiation history but is not the document used to set the final figure.

3. **Matter closing memorandum:**
   - `documents/matters/1021-00006/Client Reporting/matter-closing-memorandum.docx`
   - This memorandum identifies the same case, describes the approximately **$150 million** damages claim and the settlement disposition, and records that the matter was closed after the filing and entry of a dismissal with prejudice on April 26, 2024. The $150 million figure is the claim/exposure figure—not the executed settlement amount.

4. **Settlement term sheet:**
   - `documents/matters/1021-00006/Mediation & Settlement/settlement-term-sheet.docx`
   - The March 22, 2024 term sheet states the same proposed **$87.5 million** total consideration, but expressly says it is non-binding except for specified provisions. It is therefore corroborative only; the executed settlement agreement controls.

## Reasoning and treatment of amounts

I compared the monetary terms in executed settlement agreements and mutual releases across the settlement-related matters, using the fixed amount the operative executed instrument defines as the settlement amount. I did **not** treat the following as separate or additional settlements:

- pleaded damages, claimed exposure, or counterclaims;
- settlement authority ranges, offers, term sheets, drafts, or negotiation positions;
- collateral values or the value of non-monetary relief;
- interest accruing under a payment schedule; or
- multiple payment tranches within one agreement as multiple settlements.

Thus, the $25 million closing payment and $62.5 million structured-payment principal are added **once** because the agreement expressly defines their aggregate as $87.5 million. The agreement separately provides for **6.5% simple interest** on the outstanding structured-payment balance, but that is an ancillary payment term and is not included in the agreement’s defined “Settlement Amount.” Likewise, the agreement’s $150 million damages claim and the $12 million counterclaim are not added to the settlement figure; both are claims resolved/released by the agreement.

As cross-checks, other executed instruments reviewed include:

- `documents/matters/1033-00006/Settlement Documents/settlement-agreement-execution.docx`, which defines a **$14,750,000** settlement amount;
- `documents/matters/1017-00004/Mediation & Settlement/Class Action/class-settlement-agreement-execution.docx`, which defines a **$14,750,000** gross settlement amount (with a separate executed Aldrich agreement in that matter defining a $2,350,000 settlement payment);
